name: Gran Paradiso National Park
blurb: Ibex saved from extinction, whistling marmots and eagles above the Alpine treeline.

tip.title: Take away the snow
tip.text: Snowmelt waters the short alpine growing season. Set Snow cover to -100% and watch the grasses and sedges, then the ibex, marmots and the wolves and eagles that hunt them.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Alpine meadow-grass
nodes.desc: Common grass of alpine pastures. Poa is among the grass genera that make up the bulk of the ibex diet, and GloBI records the snow vole eating it.

nodes.name: Bicoloured sedge
nodes.desc: Small sedge of damp ground near meltwater and snowbeds. GloBI records roe deer and red deer feeding on it.

nodes.name: Alpine clover
nodes.desc: Flowering legume of high pastures. Herbs like this are eaten by grazers in summer, and it is a larval food plant for the mountain clouded yellow butterfly.

nodes.name: Houseleeks
nodes.desc: Succulent rosettes on rock and thin soil. They are the caterpillar food plant of the Apollo butterfly, which also takes a bitter compound from them.

nodes.name: European larch
nodes.desc: The most common tree of the valley floors in the park, mixed with spruce and Swiss stone pine. It marks the upper forest edge.

nodes.name: Alpine ibex
nodes.desc: Wild goat of steep ground that eats mostly grasses, with herbs in summer and shrubs and conifer shoots in winter. The park protected the last animals; numbers rose from about 100 to about 4,000.

nodes.name: Chamois
nodes.desc: Mountain antelope that grazes alpine meadows in summer and moves down to forest in winter. Wolves and lynx are its historic predators.

nodes.name: Alpine marmot
nodes.desc: Colonial burrowing rodent that eats grasses and herbs, fattening up for hibernation of up to nine months. It whistles an alarm when predators appear.

nodes.name: European roe deer
nodes.desc: Small deer of the lower forests and clearings that browses leaves, shoots and herbs. GloBI records it eating bicoloured sedge.

nodes.name: Mountain hare
nodes.desc: Hare of high open ground that feeds on grasses and herbs. Recorded in the area and a main prey item of golden eagles generally.

nodes.name: European snow vole
nodes.desc: Rock-dwelling vole of high screes and boulder fields. GloBI records it eating alpine meadow-grass.

nodes.name: Apollo
nodes.desc: Large butterfly of flower-rich mountain meadows. The caterpillars eat stonecrops and houseleeks, and the adults taste bitter to predators.

nodes.name: Asp viper
nodes.desc: Venomous snake of sunny rocky slopes. GloBI records it eating voles, lizards and small mammals.

nodes.name: European badger
nodes.desc: Omnivore of lower slopes. GloBI records it eating voles, shrews, frogs and lizards.

nodes.name: Red fox
nodes.desc: Generalist hunter and scavenger. GloBI records it eating marmots, hares, voles, roe deer and ibex.

nodes.name: Grey wolf
nodes.desc: Returned to the park area from central Italy. GloBI records it eating chamois, ibex, roe deer, marmots and foxes.

nodes.name: Golden eagle
nodes.desc: Nests near the treeline and hunts the pastures above. Marmots and hares are main prey, and it can take young ibex.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Summer sun drives a short, intense growing season on the alpine slopes.

nodes.name: Snow cover
nodes.desc: Winter snow insulates plants and its melt feeds the pastures; deep snow also limits winter food for grazers.

nodes.name: Glacier meltwater
nodes.desc: The park holds 57 glaciers, and their melt waters damp meadows and streams through the summer.

nodes.name: Thin alpine soil
nodes.desc: Poor, shallow soils above the treeline; plants there are dwarfed and deep rooted.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi, bacteria and soil invertebrates that break down dead plants and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.
